End-grain cutting board · shop plan · rosettes

Hex Rosettes End-Grain Board

A rhombitrihexagonal grid like the hub-and-strut net of a geodesic frame: purpleheart hexagons, each framed by six pale maple squares, with small walnut triangles at every corner where three squares meet, so the board is a field of six-petal rosettes joined by square links. 9 rows of 6 rosettes; every edge is 0.75". Built as straight strips: the strip lines run through hexagon centres, so some hexagons are two trapezoids and some squares and triangles are halves; the halves' glue lines are same-species and disappear in end grain.

01

Overview

A rhombitrihexagonal grid like the hub-and-strut net of a geodesic frame: purpleheart hexagons, each framed by six pale maple squares, with small walnut triangles at every corner where three squares meet, so the board is a field of six-petal rosettes joined by square links
129⁄32" × 1531⁄32" × 11⁄2"
9 of 10 checks pass

About the pattern

  • 9 rows of 6 rosettes; every edge is 0.75". Built as straight strips: the strip lines run through hexagon centres, so some hexagons are two trapezoids and some squares and triangles are halves; the halves' glue lines are same-species and disappear in end grain.
  • Inside each strip the pieces nest two across, so tape-glue each strip on a full-size template, then flatten both broad faces before crosscutting.
  • Three bar shapes and three saw setups: hexagon (four 30 degree bevels), square, triangle (30 degrees).

What you'll need

  • Purpleheart: 5.5 bd ft
  • Hard maple: 6.5 bd ft
  • Black walnut: 2 bd ft

Tools

  • Table saw with a digital angle gauge (blade at 30°)
  • Thin-rip jig, zero-clearance insert, push block
  • Crosscut sled with a stop block
  • Bar clamps, cauls, packing tape for the bevelled units
  • Router sled or drum sander (not a planer)
  • Random-orbit sander, mineral oil and board butter

Board feet include 25% for defects and milling. Blanks are 51⁄2" wide after jointing; wider stock gives more bars per blank.

The woods

  • Purpleheart · Janka 2520 · shrinkage 6.4%. Vivid purple that browns with UV; very hard on tools.
  • Hard maple · Janka 1450 · shrinkage 9.9%. The standard board wood: hard, tight pores, pale.
  • Black walnut · Janka 1010 · shrinkage 7.8%. Dark contrast wood; a little soft, so keep it to accents or pair it with cherry.

Bars & rip setups

Every piece of the face is the end of one of these bars

C3⁄4" squareHard maple · square2323 @ 151⁄2"3⁄4"
Aregular hexagon, 3⁄4" sidePurpleheart · hex55 @ 151⁄2"15⁄16"
F60-degree trapezoid, 11⁄2" x 3⁄4"Purpleheart · hex1010 @ 151⁄2"21⁄32"

A

regular hexagon, 3⁄4" side

blade 30.0° from vertical
  • Mill the blank to 1.299" (≈15⁄16") thick (the hexagon across its flats) and rip strips 1.500" (≈11⁄2") wide, blade square.
  • Tilt the blade 30.0 degrees from vertical (digital angle gauge).
  • Bevel all four long corners of each strip: with a flat face on the table and the fence set so the cut meets the edge at mid-thickness, rip, turn the strip end for end, rip, then flip it over and repeat. Every face is then 0.750" (≈3⁄4").
  • Make a test bar first and check every corner is 120 degrees; a hexagon that is off shows at every joint.
B

3⁄8" x 3⁄4" rectangle

blade square
  • Mill the blank to 0.375" (≈3⁄8") thick.
  • Rip bars 0.750" (≈3⁄4") wide, blade square to the table.
C

3⁄4" square

blade square
  • Mill the blank to 0.750" (≈3⁄4") thick.
  • Rip bars 0.750" (≈3⁄4") wide, blade square to the table.
D

equilateral triangle, 3⁄4" base

blade 30.0° from vertical
  • Mill the blank to 0.650" (≈21⁄32") thick (the triangle's height).
  • Tilt the blade 30.0 degrees and rip the first bevel; discard the strip.
  • Flip the blank over (face for face) before every pass so the bevels alternate; each pass releases a triangle 0.750" (≈3⁄4") across its base with the base on the table side of the cut.
  • Check: equal sides 0.750" (≈3⁄4"), apex 60.0 degrees.
E

30⁄60-degree right triangle, 3⁄8" x 21⁄32"

blade 30.0° from vertical
  • Mill the blank to 0.650" (≈21⁄32") thick and rip strips 0.375" (≈3⁄8") wide, blade square: each strip is two triangles' rectangle stood on edge.
  • Tilt the blade 30.0 degrees from vertical (digital angle gauge) and rip each strip corner to corner (stand it on its narrow face against the fence, set so the cut runs from the top far corner to the bottom near corner). Both halves are the bar; mark the off-fence half so it isn't lost.
  • Check: legs 0.375" (≈3⁄8") and 0.650" (≈21⁄32"), hypotenuse 0.750" (≈3⁄4"), corners 90, 60.0 and 30.0 degrees.
F

60-degree trapezoid, 11⁄2" x 3⁄4"

blade 30.0° from vertical
  • Mill the blank to 0.650" (≈21⁄32") thick (the trapezoid's height).
  • Tilt the blade 30.0 degrees from vertical (digital angle gauge) and rip the first bevel; discard the strip.
  • Flip the blank over (face for face) before every pass so the bevels alternate; set the fence so each pass releases a trapezoid 1.500" (≈11⁄2") across its wide face and 0.750" (≈3⁄4") across its narrow face.
  • Check: 60.0 degree base corners, slanted sides 0.750" (≈3⁄4").

06

Building it

In order, with the reason where it isn't obvious
7 steps
  1. 1

    Buy and acclimate the lumber

    • Buy the boards in the material list (Purpleheart, Hard maple, Black walnut) and let them sit in the shop a week, stickered.
    • Pick straight-grained, quartersawn or rift stock for the bars where you can: it moves less and the end grain shows tight, even rings.
  2. 2

    Rip the bars

    • Joint and plane every blank flat and to its exact thickness (material list). Bars of one shape must come from blanks planed in the same session at the same setting, or they won't match.
    • Bar A (regular hexagon, 3⁄4" side): Mill the blank to 1.299" (≈15⁄16") thick (the hexagon across its flats) and rip strips 1.500" (≈11⁄2") wide, blade square. Tilt the blade 30.0 degrees from vertical (digital angle gauge). Bevel all four long corners of each strip: with a flat face on the table and the fence set so the cut meets the edge at mid-thickness, rip, turn the strip end for end, rip, then flip it over and repeat. Every face is then 0.750" (≈3⁄4"). Make a test bar first and check every corner is 120 degrees; a hexagon that is off shows at every joint.
    • Bar B (3⁄8" x 3⁄4" rectangle): Mill the blank to 0.375" (≈3⁄8") thick. Rip bars 0.750" (≈3⁄4") wide, blade square to the table.
    • Bar C (3⁄4" square): Mill the blank to 0.750" (≈3⁄4") thick. Rip bars 0.750" (≈3⁄4") wide, blade square to the table.
    • Bar D (equilateral triangle, 3⁄4" base): Mill the blank to 0.650" (≈21⁄32") thick (the triangle's height). Tilt the blade 30.0 degrees and rip the first bevel; discard the strip. Flip the blank over (face for face) before every pass so the bevels alternate; each pass releases a triangle 0.750" (≈3⁄4") across its base with the base on the table side of the cut. Check: equal sides 0.750" (≈3⁄4"), apex 60.0 degrees.
    • Bar E (30⁄60-degree right triangle, 3⁄8" x 21⁄32"): Mill the blank to 0.650" (≈21⁄32") thick and rip strips 0.375" (≈3⁄8") wide, blade square: each strip is two triangles' rectangle stood on edge. Tilt the blade 30.0 degrees from vertical (digital angle gauge) and rip each strip corner to corner (stand it on its narrow face against the fence, set so the cut runs from the top far corner to the bottom near corner). Both halves are the bar; mark the off-fence half so it isn't lost. Check: legs 0.375" (≈3⁄8") and 0.650" (≈21⁄32"), hypotenuse 0.750" (≈3⁄4"), corners 90, 60.0 and 30.0 degrees.
    • Bar F (60-degree trapezoid, 11⁄2" x 3⁄4"): Mill the blank to 0.650" (≈21⁄32") thick (the trapezoid's height). Tilt the blade 30.0 degrees from vertical (digital angle gauge) and rip the first bevel; discard the strip. Flip the blank over (face for face) before every pass so the bevels alternate; set the fence so each pass releases a trapezoid 1.500" (≈11⁄2") across its wide face and 0.750" (≈3⁄4") across its narrow face. Check: 60.0 degree base corners, slanted sides 0.750" (≈3⁄4").
    • Rip every bar of a shape in one session without touching the saw setup, and rip 10% spares. Dry-fit the first few bars into a unit or a short row before ripping the rest: half a degree of bevel error doubles at every joint and opens gaps across a row.
    See sheet 03
    DON'Ttouch the blade tilt or the thin-rip jig partway through a shape. Bars from two setups never meet cleanly; rip every bar of a shape, plus spares, in one run.
  3. 3
    1ST GLUE-UP

    Glue the logs

    • Log L: 75 bars glued as drawn (where bars sit side by side, glue those groups first and clean their joint face), into a panel 2.049" (≈21⁄16") thick (one strip of the board) by about 1715⁄32" wide; make 1, 15.500" (≈151⁄2") long, for 7 slices plus 1 spare.
    • Lay the bars on a waxed, flat caul against a straight fence, in the drawn order, and glue four to six at a time. Clamp lightly along the stack, and clamp cauls down across both faces so a bevelled joint can't ride up.
    • Take the squeeze-out off while it is rubbery (20 to 40 minutes): it peels off a flat bevel with a chisel or a plastic scraper, where cured glue would need cutting. Add the next section once the last has set.
    • When the panel is done, scrape or drum-sand both broad faces just flat: these are the glue faces for the board. Take off only glue and lips; every 1⁄32" removed narrows this strip of the pattern. Check that the panel is 2.049" (≈21⁄16") thick everywhere and flat under a straightedge.
    See sheet 04
    DON'Tglue a whole panel at once or let squeeze-out cure on a bevel. Fresh squeeze-out peels off; cured glue on a bevel has to be pared, and paring changes the angle.
  4. 4

    Crosscut the slices

    • Before cutting, draw a pencil V across the top of each log: every slice keeps a mark that says which way is up and where it came from.
    • On a crosscut sled with a stop block, cut slices 1.625" (≈15⁄8") thick (finished 11⁄2" plus 1⁄8" to flatten). Hold the off-cut side with a hold-down, never the fence side.
    • Cut 8 slices in all; stack them in order.
  5. 5
    2ND GLUE-UP

    Glue the board

    • Lay out the 7 slices as numbered in the layout drawing. Every slice goes down as cut. Dry-fit the whole board and look at it before any glue.
    • Glue in stages of two to four slices, then glue the stages together. End grain drinks glue: brush a thin coat on both faces, wait two minutes, add a second coat, then clamp with moderate pressure and cauls top and bottom so the slices stay flush (the faces are end grain and are hard to plane flat).
    • Every slice is a straight strip with flat faces. Line each one up with its neighbour by the pattern, not the ends (the ends are ragged and get trimmed): dry-fit, then mark across each joint with a pencil tick so the strips go back in register under glue.
    See sheet 05
    DON'Tglue all the slices at once. With more than four joints the slices creep out of plane under clamp pressure, and end grain is slow to flatten.
  6. 6

    Trim and flatten

    • Trim to 12.294" (≈129⁄32") x 15.971" (≈1531⁄32") on the red lines (crosscut sled or track saw, with a backer to stop breakout).
    • Flatten both faces with a router sled or a drum sander. Do not run end grain through a thickness planer: it blows out the trailing edge and can throw pieces.
    • Sand both faces 80, 120, 180; wipe with a damp cloth to raise the grain, let dry, sand 220.
    See sheet 01
    DON'Trun the board through a thickness planer. End grain blows out at the trailing edge and the planer can throw pieces.
  7. 7

    Edges, feet and finish

    • Ease every edge with a 1⁄8" chamfer and break the corners: end-grain edges chip if left sharp.
    • Add four rubber feet with stainless screws, inset 1" from the corners (feet let the board dry evenly underneath).
    • Flood with food-grade mineral oil until it stops soaking in (end grain takes a lot: several coats over two days), then buff on a board butter of mineral oil and beeswax. Re-oil monthly.
